purpose: Lovastatin is used to lower your 'bad' cholesterol (LDL) and triglycerides, while raising your 'good' cholesterol (HDL). It helps reduce the amount of fatty buildup in your blood vessels. This lowers your risk of heart attack, stroke, and other heart problems.
how_it_works: Your liver naturally makes cholesterol, and lovastatin works by blocking a key enzyme your liver uses to produce it. Think of it like putting a speed limiter on a cholesterol-making machine inside your body. With less cholesterol being made, your liver pulls more of the bad cholesterol out of your blood, which lowers your overall cholesterol levels.
common_side_effects: The most common side effects include muscle aches or weakness, upset stomach, nausea, gas, constipation, or diarrhea. Some people may notice headaches or trouble sleeping. Most side effects are mild, but let your doctor know if anything bothers you.
warnings: The most important warning is muscle damage — if you have unusual muscle pain, weakness, or dark-colored urine, call your doctor right away, as this can be serious. Do not drink large amounts of grapefruit juice, as it can increase the drug in your body to unsafe levels. Avoid this medication if you are pregnant or breastfeeding, as it can harm a baby. Tell your doctor about all other medications you take, since many drugs can interact with lovastatin.
typical_dosing: The usual starting dose is 20 mg once a day, taken with your evening meal. Your doctor may adjust your dose between 10 mg and 80 mg per day depending on how your cholesterol responds. Taking it with food, especially in the evening, helps it work best since your body makes the most cholesterol at night.
